questions.question_text: Which of the following describes why the parabola $y = 16 - x^2$ does NOT have an inverse function?

options.text: A horizontal line such as $y = 0$ intersects the curve at two points ($x = -4$ and $x = 4$).
A vertical line such as $x = 0$ intersects the curve at two points.
options.why: Confused the horizontal line test for injectivity with the vertical line test for a relation being a function.

options.text: The graph has a maximum turning point at $(0, 16)$ rather than passing through the origin.
options.why: Believed having a non-zero $y$-intercept or turning point prevents an inverse function from existing.

options.text: The domain of the parabola is restricted to positive real numbers.
options.why: Assumed the parabola has a restricted domain rather than $(-\infty, \infty)$ where it fails the horizontal line test.

questions.solution_text:
For a function to have an inverse function, it must be one-to-one and pass the horizontal line test.
For $y = 16 - x^2$, the horizontal line $y = 0$ crosses at $x = -4$ and $x = 4$.
Because a horizontal line intersects the curve more than once, it fails the horizontal line test.

questions.question_text: Which of the following relations is classified as one-to-one?

options.why: A parabola is many-to-one because two $x$-values produce the same $y$-value.
A sideways parabola is one-to-many because one $x$-value produces two $y$-values.
A circle fails both vertical and horizontal line tests, making it many-to-many.

questions.solution_text:
$y = 3x - 5$ is a non-horizontal straight line.
It passes both the vertical line test (each $x$ has one $y$) and the horizontal line test (each $y$ has one $x$).
Therefore, it is a one-to-one relation.

questions.question_text: If $f(x) = |2x - 6|$, which pair of $x$-values demonstrates that $f(x)$ is NOT one-to-one?

options.why: Evaluated $f(0) = 6$ and $f(2) = 2$, which gives $6 \neq 2$ and does not show equal outputs.
Evaluated $f(3) = 0$ and $f(-3) = 12$, which gives $0 \neq 12$ and does not demonstrate many-to-one mapping.
Evaluated $f(2) = 2$ and $f(-2) = 10$, which gives $2 \neq 10$ and does not produce equal function outputs.

questions.question_text: Under what condition will the inverse relation of a given function $y = f(x)$ be a function?

options.text: Every horizontal line intersects the graph of $y = f(x)$ at most once.
Every vertical line intersects the graph of $y = f(x)$ at least once.
options.why: Confused the horizontal line test with a condition for the domain being all real numbers.

options.text: The graph of $y = f(x)$ is symmetric about the $y$-axis.
options.why: Symmetry about the $y$-axis describes an even function, which is many-to-one and fails the horizontal line test.

options.text: The function has at least one real root where $f(x) = 0$.
options.why: Having a root is irrelevant to whether a function is one-to-one.

questions.solution_text:
An inverse relation is a function if and only if the original function is one-to-one.
A function is one-to-one if and only if every horizontal line intersects its graph at most once (horizontal line test).

questions.question_text: For the cubic function $f(x) = x^3 - 9x$, which of the following confirms that $f(x)$ does not possess an inverse function?

options.why: Miscalculated $f(1) = 1 - 9 = -8$ and $f(-1) = -1 + 9 = 8$; they are negatives of each other, not equal.
Incorrectly claimed the cubic has only one intercept when it actually has three ($x = -3, 0, 3$).
The derivative $3x^2 - 9$ changes sign, and a strictly negative derivative would make the function one-to-one.

questions.solution_text:
$f(-3) = (-3)^3 - 9(-3) = -27 + 27 = 0$
$f(0) = 0$
$f(3) = 3^3 - 9(3) = 27 - 27 = 0$
Three distinct $x$-values produce the same output $0$, so $f(x)$ is not one-to-one.

options.why: Looked only at lines near the top of the curve rather than the region between the local minimum and local maximum.
Assumed the function is one-to-one without checking lines across the central polynomial wave.
Counted turning points instead of maximum line intersections across the quartic curve.

questions.solution_text:
The quartic curve has two local minima at $y = 1$ (at $x = \pm 1$) and a local maximum at $(0, 2)$.
A horizontal line with $1 < y < 2$ (such as $y = 1.5$) crosses all 4 upward branches.
Therefore, the maximum number of intersections is $4$.

questions.question_text: Consider the function $f(x) = \dfrac{4x + 1}{2x - 3}$ for $x \neq \frac{3}{2}$. Which algebraic statement proves that $f(x)$ is one-to-one?

options.text: Setting $f(a) = f(b)$ leads uniquely to $a = b$.

options.why: The function is not odd; proving odd parity does not guarantee injectivity anyway.

options.text: The denominator $2x - 3 \neq 0$ has only one real zero.
options.why: Having a single vertical asymptote does not establish that distinct inputs give distinct outputs.
A single point evaluation cannot prove a global property like injectivity.

questions.solution_text:
A function is one-to-one if $f(a) = f(b) \implies a = b$ for all $a, b$ in the domain.
$\dfrac{4a + 1}{2a - 3} = \dfrac{4b + 1}{2b - 3}$
$(4a + 1)(2b - 3) = (4b + 1)(2a - 3)$
$8ab - 12a + 2b - 3 = 8ab - 12b + 2a - 3$
$-14a = -14b \implies a = b$
Since $f(a) = f(b)$ strictly requires $a = b$, $f(x)$ is one-to-one.

questions.question_text: A relation is defined by the equation $y^2 = 8x$ for $x \ge 0$. If this relation is reflected in the line $y = x$, what type of relation is the resulting reflection?

options.why: The original relation $y^2 = 8x$ is one-to-many; its reflection swaps input and output to become many-to-one.
Failed to notice that the reflected parabola $x^2 = 8y$ maps two $x$-values ($x$ and $-x$) to the same $y$-value.
The reflection $y = \frac{1}{8}x^2$ is a standard vertical parabola, which is a function, not many-to-many.

questions.solution_text:
The original relation $y^2 = 8x$ is a horizontal parabola: it is one-to-many (fails VLT, passes HLT).
Reflecting in $y = x$ interchanges $x$ and $y$, giving $x^2 = 8y \iff y = \frac{1}{8}x^2$.
$y = \frac{1}{8}x^2$ is a standard vertical parabola.
It passes the vertical line test (is a function) but fails the horizontal line test (since $(\pm a)^2 = a^2$).
Therefore, the reflected relation is many-to-one.
